## Course overview

Tiny machine learning places models on embedded devices that collect and process
sensor data under limits on memory, computation, and power. Harvard CS249r
connects those constraints to the design of a complete system, from data
collection and model training to deployment on a microcontroller.

The course combines research discussions with programming assignments and a
final project. Topics include embedded ML frameworks, model compression,
benchmarking, and low-power system design. The original course websites preserve
the requirements and materials for each offering.

## Course assignments on GitHub

- **[CS249r course repository](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r).**
  The Harvard Edge repository links the early book and semester assignment
  repositories through its
  [submodule configuration](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r/blob/main/.gitmodules).
- **[Fall 2020 assignment seed](https://github.com/Harvard-CS249R-Fall2020/assignments).**
  Public assignment starters for hello world, gesture recognition, person
  detection, wake words, and responsible AI. The repository includes the original
  GitHub Classroom workflow used by the course.
- **[Fall 2022 Assignment 2](https://github.com/mmaz/cs249r-a2).**
  The repository identifies the semester in its README and is linked from the
  course repository. It contains the assignment notebook, training and
  quantization scripts, and deployment resources for visual wake words/person
  detection. [Open its notebook in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/mmaz/cs249r-a2/blob/master/cs249r_a2.ipynb).

## Selected example projects

The selected course projects below connect data collection, model training,
and hardware deployment. Their original repositories preserve the code and
project documentation.

### Cache 4 Trash

[Project repository](https://github.com/AditiR-42/cache-4-trash) ·
[Course showcase](https://sites.google.com/g.harvard.edu/cs249-tinyml-2023/fall-2023-final-projects)

A waste-sorting system combines classification on Nicla Vision with a motorized
sorting mechanism. The repository includes dataset preparation, augmentation,
model deployment, firmware, and hardware diagrams.

### Activity recognition and ultrasound power control

[Project repository](https://github.com/euranofshin/ultrasound-power-tinyml)

The project connects activity recognition with ultrasound power control. Its
repository includes activity data, a Nicla Vision inference sketch, experiment
plotting scripts, and documentation of the ultrasound connection.

### Air Guitar

[Project repository](https://github.com/RobJMal/Air-Guitar-CS249R)

Motion and finger-flex sensors provide inputs to a gesture-recognition model
on a Teensy board. The repository includes data-collection code, training
notebooks, deployment code, and hardware schematics.

## Related HarvardX TinyML materials

The HarvardX/edX specialization is a separate teaching program. Its public
materials complement the campus course archive:

- **[TinyMLx courseware](https://github.com/tinyMLx/courseware/tree/master/edX):**
  course structure, slides, and readings for the HarvardX specialization.
- **[TinyMLx Colab notebooks](https://github.com/tinyMLx/colabs):** notebooks for
  the edX TinyML specialization.
- **[Harvard TinyMLx Arduino library](https://github.com/tinyMLx/arduino-library):**
  source code and examples for the TinyML kit and shield.

The [TinyMLedu teaching page](https://tinyml.seas.harvard.edu/teach/) connects
these materials with the Harvard campus offerings and a wider teaching community.

## For instructors {#for-instructors}

The [adaptable TinyML syllabus](https://mlsysbook.ai/instructors/tinyml-syllabus.html)
provides a teaching plan for embedded machine learning with Volume I as a
companion reference. Its schedule is a reusable template, separate from the
historical Harvard offerings listed here. The
[Instructor Hub](https://mlsysbook.ai/instructors/) also provides guidance on
pedagogy, assessment, and course adaptation.

## Connection to the textbook

TinyML makes memory, energy, and latency constraints visible on a small device.
[Introduction to Machine Learning Systems](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/) develops
the broader principles behind those constraints, including model compression,
hardware acceleration, and deployment. The original Harvard materials provide
examples of applying those principles on microcontrollers.

Other learning paths and courses at other institutions are listed in the
[course directory](../index.qmd).
